subject: Cooking
title: How a Goat Discovered Coffee
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: How a Goat Discovered Coffee.

hook.text: Legend says an Ethiopian goat herder noticed his goats dancing after eating red berries. Coffee was born.

buildup.text: Kaldi — the mythical herder — brought the berries to a monk, who brewed them and stayed awake all night.

discovery.text: Coffee originated in Ethiopia's Kaffa region — wild coffee plants still grow there in ancient forests.

twist.text: Coffee wasn't brewed at first. Ethiopians mixed crushed beans with animal fat to create energy balls.

climax.text: By the 15th century, coffee reached Yemen's Sufi monks, who used it for nightlong prayer sessions.

punchline.text: Dancing goats led to the world's most consumed psychoactive substance.

details.summary: Legend says an Ethiopian goatherd named Kaldi noticed his goats dancing after eating red cherries from a wild bush around 850 CE. He brought the cherries to a monastery where monks brewed them to stay awake for prayers.
details.whyItMatters: The Kaldi legend anchors coffee's identity to Ethiopia, where wild coffee trees still grow. It is the origin story that launched a commodity worth over $100 billion annually.
takeaways: The legend of Kaldi places coffee origins in Ethiopia around 850 CE
Wild coffee still grows in Ethiopian highland forests today
Monks may have been among the first to brew coffee for alertness

faq.question: Is the Kaldi goat herder story actually true?
faq.answer: Almost certainly not in its specific details. The story first appeared in writing in the 17th century, over 800 years after its supposed occurrence. However, the story correctly identifies Ethiopia as coffee's homeland. Wild Coffea arabica plants are native to Ethiopian forests.

faq.question: Where in Ethiopia did coffee actually originate?
faq.answer: Coffee is native to the forests of southwestern Ethiopia, particularly the Kaffa region — which may be the source of the word coffee. Wild coffee plants still grow in these forests. Ethiopia remains the only country where coffee grows wild rather than being cultivated.
